    Significance test for the baseline PIT-Wasserstein metric

    b_pit_significance.Rd

    Tests the strongest of the three null hypotheses in the PIT-Wasserstein family: that the predictions are fully probabilistically calibrated, so that the raw PIT values are i.i.d. \(U(0,1)\) — correct location and correct dispersion and correct shape. The test is one-sided: B_pit is a distance, so only large values are evidence against calibration.

    b_pit_significance(B_pit, n_predictions)

    Arguments

    B_pit

    the baseline (unadjusted) PIT-Wasserstein metric, reported as B_pit by pit_w() and prediction_scores()

    n_predictions

    the number of predictions each B_pit was computed from, as returned by prediction_scores()

    Value

    a dataframe with one row per input value and columns:

    • B_pit, n_predictions — as supplied

    • statistic — \(\sqrt{n}\,B_{pit}\), the quantity with a fixed null

    • expected — the null mean of B_pit, \(\sqrt{2\pi}/(8\sqrt{n})\)

    • critical_0.05 — the one-sided 5% critical value of B_pit

    • p_value — the probability of a B_pit at least this large under full probabilistic calibration

    Details

    Under that null \(\sqrt{n}\,B_{pit}\) converges to \(\int_0^1|B^\circ|\), the integrated absolute Brownian bridge, whose c.d.f. is p_l1_bridge(). Nothing is estimated from the data, so the null is exact and fully analytical.

    B_pit rejects when anything is wrong and says nothing about what. Use it as the omnibus first stage, then d_pit_significance() to test dispersion free of any location error, and u_pit_significance() for the residual shape.

    Unit tests

    

# a calibrated forecaster sits near the null mean and is not significant
res = b_pit_significance(sqrt(2 * pi) / 8 / sqrt(100), 100)
testthat::expect_true(res$p_value > 0.3)

# the 5% critical value has, by construction, a p value of 0.05
crit = b_pit_significance(0, 100)$critical_0.05
testthat::expect_equal(b_pit_significance(crit, 100)$p_value, 0.05, tolerance = 1e-5)

# the critical value scales as 1/sqrt(n)
testthat::expect_equal(
  b_pit_significance(0, 400)$critical_0.05 * 2,
  b_pit_significance(0, 100)$critical_0.05,
  tolerance = 1e-6
)

# and is strictly larger than the adjusted test's, which has estimated a
# location parameter from the same data
testthat::expect_true(
  b_pit_significance(0, 100)$critical_0.05 > u_pit_significance(0, 100)$critical_0.05
)

# vectorised over both arguments
testthat::expect_equal(nrow(b_pit_significance(c(0.02, 0.09), c(76, 76))), 2L)
